title: Malaria and Dengue: Biotechnology Against Mosquito-borne Disease
subtitle: Same mosquito delivery, completely different biology
subject: Biology
syllabusDotPoints: investigate and analyse the wide range of interrelated factors involved in limiting local, regional and global spread of a named infectious disease
interpret data relating to the incidence and prevalence of infectious disease in populations, for example: Malaria or Dengue Fever in South East Asia
Conduct a secondary-source investigation to evaluate the use of biotechnologies on the prevalence of mosquito-borne diseases
inquiryQuestion: How can the spread of infectious diseases be controlled?
lessonIntent: Students can describe the Plasmodium life cycle and dengue serotype biology, and evaluate biotechnologies such as Wolbachia, malaria vaccines and gene drives using evidence on the prevalence of mosquito-borne disease.
examSkill: Evaluate a biotechnology against a mosquito-borne disease using incidence and prevalence evidence, and explain why dengue is hard to vaccinate against.

introVoiceover.text: Welcome back to HSC Biology. Today, malaria, dengue and the biotechnologies fighting them. Let's get into it.

scenes.caption: Malaria and Dengue: Biotechnology Against Mosquito-borne Disease (Year 12 Biology, Module 7, Lesson 18)

scenes.heading: Hundreds of thousands of deaths a year
scenes.body: In 2021 malaria caused about 247 million cases and 619,000 deaths. We have nets, drugs, even vaccines. Why isn't it gone?
scenes.callout: Why is a parasite that needs a mosquito so impossible to eradicate?
scenes.caption: Malaria still kills hundreds of thousands a year despite every available tool.

voiceover.text: OK, here's a sobering set of numbers. The World Health Organization estimated that in twenty twenty one, malaria caused about two hundred and forty seven million cases and six hundred and nineteen thousand deaths, most of them young children in Africa. And we're not helpless against it. We have insecticide treated bed nets, effective antimalarial drugs, and after decades of work, vaccines. Yet the parasite keeps killing. Meanwhile dengue, spread by a different mosquito, is surging across South East Asia and beyond. Today we use malaria and dengue as a case study, two diseases delivered by mosquitoes but with completely different biology, and we'll evaluate the biotechnologies being used to bring their numbers down.

scenes.heading: Malaria: a parasite with a life cycle
scenes.body: Malaria is not a virus or a bacterium. It is caused by Plasmodium, a eukaryotic parasite with a multi-stage life cycle.

bullets.text: Spread by female Anopheles mosquitoes, which bite at night. P. falciparum is the most lethal species.
Its life cycle runs mosquito, then liver (silent), then blood (the fever and symptoms).
Each stage is a separate intervention point: nets for the mosquito, drugs for the blood stage.

scenes.secondary: Because Plasmodium is a complex eukaryote, antibiotics and antivirals do not touch it. Antimalarial drugs target parasite-specific processes.
scenes.callout: A multi-stage life cycle means multiple places to attack it.
scenes.caption: Malaria is caused by the eukaryotic parasite Plasmodium, with mosquito, liver and blood stages.

voiceover.text: Let's start with malaria, and the first thing to get right is what causes it. Malaria isn't a virus or a bacterium. It's caused by Plasmodium, a single celled eukaryotic parasite. It's spread by female Anopheles mosquitoes, which tend to bite at night, and the deadliest species is Plasmodium falciparum. The key is its life cycle. The mosquito injects the parasite, which travels first to the liver, where it multiplies silently, and then it bursts into the blood, invading red blood cells and causing the cycles of fever, anaemia and organ damage. Each stage is a separate point of attack. Bed nets target the mosquito, antimalarial drugs target the blood stage, and vaccines aim at the parasite as it heads for the liver. And because Plasmodium is a eukaryote, antibiotics and antivirals do nothing against it.

scenes.heading: The words you need

bullets.text: Plasmodium: the eukaryotic parasite that causes malaria, with mosquito, liver and blood stages.
Serotype: a distinct variant of a pathogen; dengue virus has four (DENV-1 to DENV-4).
Antibody-dependent enhancement: where antibodies from one dengue serotype worsen infection by another.
Wolbachia: a natural bacterium that reduces a mosquito's ability to transmit dengue.

scenes.callout: Four dengue serotypes, and immunity to one is not immunity to all.
scenes.caption: Plasmodium, serotype, antibody-dependent enhancement, Wolbachia.

voiceover.text: Let's pin down the key terms. Plasmodium is the eukaryotic parasite that causes malaria, with those mosquito, liver and blood stages. A serotype is a distinct variant of a pathogen, and dengue virus comes in four serotypes, labelled DENV one through four. Antibody dependent enhancement, or ADE, is a counterintuitive effect where antibodies left over from one dengue serotype make a later infection by a different serotype worse, not better. And Wolbachia is a natural bacterium that, when established in Aedes mosquitoes, reduces their ability to transmit dengue. The big idea to hold onto, with dengue, immunity to one serotype is not immunity to all.

scenes.heading: Dengue: four serotypes and a paradox
scenes.body: Dengue is a virus with four serotypes, and a second infection can be worse than the first.

bullets.text: Spread by Aedes aegypti, a daytime, urban mosquito that breeds in small water containers.
One infection gives lifelong immunity to that serotype only, not the other three.
A second infection with a different serotype can trigger antibody-dependent enhancement and severe dengue.

scenes.secondary: This is the vaccine paradox: a dengue vaccine must protect against all four serotypes equally, or it can prime ADE, which is exactly what harmed seronegative children given Dengvaxia.
scenes.callout: The second dengue infection can be the dangerous one.
scenes.caption: Dengue has four serotypes; a second infection can trigger ADE and severe disease.

voiceover.text: Now dengue, which behaves completely differently. Dengue is caused by a virus, spread by Aedes aegypti, an urban, daytime biter that breeds in tiny pools of water, like a bottle cap or a plant pot. There are four serotypes, and catching one gives you lifelong immunity to that serotype only. You're still susceptible to the other three. And it gets worse. If you later catch a different serotype, the leftover antibodies can bind the new virus without neutralising it, and actually help it infect your cells. That's antibody dependent enhancement, and it can cause severe, life threatening dengue. So a dengue vaccine has to protect against all four serotypes, or it risks setting someone up for ADE, which is what happened with the Dengvaxia vaccine in children who'd never had dengue.

scenes.heading: Explain the dengue vaccine paradox
scenes.question: A child who has never had dengue is given a dengue vaccine, then later catches dengue and develops severe disease. Using serotypes and ADE, explain why vaccinating dengue-naive children can backfire.
scenes.coachNote: Link the vaccine priming a partial response to the ADE mechanism on later infection.
steps: Dengue has four serotypes; immunity to one does not protect against the others.
In a dengue-naive child, the vaccine can act like a first exposure, priming non-neutralising antibodies.
When a real, different serotype arrives, those antibodies bind it but fail to neutralise it.
Instead they help the virus enter immune cells, the ADE effect, amplifying the infection.
Answer: the vaccine mimicked a first infection, so a later serotype triggered ADE and severe dengue ✓
scenes.caption: Vaccinating dengue-naive children can prime ADE on a later infection.

voiceover.text: Let's reason through the dengue vaccine paradox properly. A child who has never had dengue is given the vaccine, then later catches dengue and develops severe disease. Why can vaccinating dengue naive children backfire? Step one, dengue has four serotypes, and immunity to one doesn't protect against the others. Step two, in a child who's never had dengue, the vaccine acts a bit like a first infection, priming antibodies that may not fully neutralise every serotype. Step three, when a real infection arrives, those antibodies bind the virus but can't neutralise it. Step four, they actually help the virus into immune cells, which is antibody dependent enhancement, and it amplifies the infection. So the vaccine mimicked a first infection, setting the child up for severe dengue. That's why Dengvaxia is now only recommended for people with confirmed past dengue.

scenes.heading: Evaluating biotechnologies
scenes.body: The test of a biotechnology is whether it measurably lowers the incidence or prevalence of disease.

bullets.text: Wolbachia mosquitoes: in a Yogyakarta trial, dengue cases fell by about 77 percent.
Malaria vaccines: RTS,S and R21 are recommended by WHO; they reduce but do not stop malaria.
Gene drives: collapsed caged Anopheles populations in the lab, but no wild release yet.

scenes.secondary: Strong evidence comes from randomised trials that compare treated and untreated areas or groups, not from before-and-after counts alone.
scenes.callout: Judge it by the data: did cases actually fall?
scenes.caption: Wolbachia cut dengue in a randomised trial; malaria vaccines give partial protection; gene drives are still experimental.

voiceover.text: So, how do we evaluate the biotechnologies aimed at these diseases? The test is always the data. Did incidence or prevalence actually fall? Start with Wolbachia. Mosquitoes carrying it were released across parts of Yogyakarta, in Indonesia, in a randomised trial, and dengue cases in treated areas fell by about seventy seven percent compared with untreated areas, with far fewer hospital admissions. Similar releases in Townsville were followed by local dengue transmission almost disappearing. For malaria, the vaccines RTS,S and R21 are now recommended by the World Health Organization for young children. They reduce cases and severe malaria, but they don't give complete protection, so they're used alongside nets and drugs. And gene drives have collapsed caged populations of malaria mosquitoes in the lab, but haven't been released into the wild, so their real effect on prevalence is still unknown.

rows: About 77% fewer cases in an RCT
Lab cages only; not yet released

scenes.heading: Two traps
scenes.body: Trap 1: thinking malaria is caused by a virus or bacterium. It is a eukaryotic parasite, Plasmodium, so antibiotics and antivirals do not work on it.
scenes.secondary: Trap 2: thinking one dengue infection makes you immune to all dengue. It only protects against that one serotype, and a second infection with another serotype can be more severe via ADE.
scenes.mistakeTag: What malaria is, and dengue immunity
scenes.callout: Malaria is a parasite, not a microbe; dengue immunity is serotype-specific.
scenes.caption: Malaria is a eukaryotic parasite; dengue immunity is serotype-specific.

voiceover.text: Two traps that cost marks. Trap one, writing that malaria is caused by a virus or a bacterium. It's neither. Malaria is caused by Plasmodium, a eukaryotic parasite, so antibiotics don't work on it, and neither do antivirals. You need antimalarial drugs that target the parasite's own machinery. Trap two, thinking that catching dengue once makes you immune to dengue forever. You only become immune to the serotype you caught, and a second infection with a different serotype can be more severe, because of antibody dependent enhancement. So prior dengue isn't simply protection, it can actually be a risk factor.

scenes.heading: Quick check
scenes.question: In a trial, dengue incidence in Wolbachia release areas was compared with nearby areas with no releases, allocated at random. Explain why this design gives stronger evidence than simply comparing a city's dengue cases before and after release.
answerSteps: Dengue incidence naturally rises and falls from year to year, with weather and serotype changes.
A before-and-after comparison can't separate the effect of Wolbachia from these other changes.
Untreated control areas experience the same weather, season and serotypes at the same time.
Random allocation of areas reduces selection bias, so the groups are comparable.
Answer: a randomised, controlled comparison isolates Wolbachia as the cause of the lower incidence ✓
scenes.caption: Random allocation and concurrent controls isolate the effect of Wolbachia on dengue incidence.

voiceover.text: Quick check. In a trial, dengue incidence in Wolbachia release areas was compared with nearby areas that had no releases, with the areas allocated at random. Explain why this gives stronger evidence than just comparing a city's dengue cases before and after release. Pause and reason it through. Right. Dengue naturally rises and falls from year to year, with the weather and with which serotypes are circulating. A before and after comparison can't separate the effect of Wolbachia from those changes. But untreated control areas go through the same weather, season and serotypes at the same time. And allocating areas at random reduces selection bias, so the groups are comparable. So the randomised, controlled comparison isolates Wolbachia as the cause of the lower incidence.

scenes.heading: Lock it in
points: Malaria is caused by Plasmodium, a eukaryotic parasite spread by night-biting Anopheles mosquitoes.
Its life cycle (mosquito, liver, blood) gives multiple intervention points: nets, drugs, vaccines.
Dengue is a virus with four serotypes spread by Aedes aegypti; a second serotype can trigger ADE.
Wolbachia mosquitoes cut dengue incidence in a randomised trial; malaria vaccines give partial protection.
Evaluate a biotechnology by the data: did incidence or prevalence fall compared with a control?
scenes.finalPrompt: Evaluating a biotechnology for a mosquito-borne disease? Name the pathogen and vector, then check the incidence data against a control.
scenes.caption: Five takeaways: Plasmodium, life-cycle targets, dengue serotypes and ADE, biotechnologies, and evidence.

voiceover.text: Let's lock it in. First, malaria is caused by Plasmodium, a eukaryotic parasite spread by night biting Anopheles mosquitoes. Second, its life cycle, mosquito, then liver, then blood, gives multiple points of attack for nets, drugs and vaccines. Third, dengue is a virus with four serotypes, spread by Aedes aegypti, and a second infection with a different serotype can trigger antibody dependent enhancement. Fourth, Wolbachia mosquitoes cut dengue incidence in a randomised trial, while malaria vaccines give real but partial protection. And fifth, evaluate any biotechnology by the data, asking whether incidence or prevalence actually fell compared with a control. See you next lesson.
